# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

### Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore structural heart interventions have revolutionized the management of cardiovascular diseases [1, 2]. While transfemoral (TF) access remains the gold standard owing to its low profile, ease of closure, and association with superior clinical outcomes, up to 10% to 15% of patients presenting for these therapies exhibit severe peripheral arterial disease, extreme vessel tortuosity, calcification, or inadequate arterial diameters that preclude a safe TF approach [3-5]. Traditionally, surgical alternatives such as transapical, transaortic, or transcarotid access were employed; however, these approaches are associated with increased morbidity, longer hospital stays, and higher mortality in fragile populations [6, 7]. Transcaval access—a completely percutaneous approach involving crossing from the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the abdominal aorta—has emerged as a highly effective alternative-access strategy that circumvents these peripheral arterial limitations while preserving the benefits of a fully percutaneous procedure [8, 9].

### Anatomical Principles and Patient Selection
Transcaval access relies on the unique anatomical relationship between the infrarenal abdominal aorta and the adjacent IVC [10]. This pathway utilizes the high-pressure gradient and surrounding retroperitoneal structures to facilitate safe access and subsequent closure [11]. Preprocedural evaluation via high-resolution computed tomography (CT) angiography is essential for patient selection and procedural planning [12]. CT imaging allows operators to identify an optimal "transcaval window" where the aorta and IVC are closely apposed, devoid of interposed structures (such as bowel loops, calcified plaques, or major renal/lumbar arteries), and free from heavy aortic calcification at the intended puncture site [13, 14].

### Procedural Technique
The procedure is performed under fluoroscopic guidance, typically using a co-axial system [15]. A standard femoral venous catheter is advanced into the IVC, and a corresponding arterial catheter is positioned in the abdominal aorta. Using an electrosurgical (Bovie) system energized with radiofrequency energy, a stiff guidewire is advanced from the IVC across the retroperitoneal space and into the abdominal aorta [16]. Once crossing is secured, a microcatheter is advanced over the wire into the aorta, and the standard crossing wire is exchanged for a super-stiff guidewire [17]. Over this wire, a large-bore sheath is advanced from the IVC into the aorta, facilitating the delivery of the structural heart device (e.g., a TAVR delivery system or mechanical circulatory support device) [18, 19].

Upon completion of the primary intervention, the aortic puncture must be closed to prevent catastrophic hemorrhage. This is achieved using an off-label nitinol-mesh vascular closure device, most commonly the Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO) [20, 21]. Under fluoroscopic and angiographic monitoring, the ADO is deployed across the caval-aortic tract, with the retention skirt positioned on the aortic side and the plug expanding within the tract and the IVC [22]. Any residual retroperitoneal bleeding is mitigated by the higher venous pressure in the IVC, which acts as a "sink," drawing any extravasated arterial blood preferentially into the low-pressure venous system rather than the retroperitoneal space [23, 24].

### Clinical Outcomes and Safety
The clinical utility of transcaval access has been validated in several key trials and registries [25, 26]. The prospective National Institutes of Health (NIH) transcaval registry demonstrated a high rate of technical success (>98%) and a 30-day survival rate comparable to or exceeding traditional surgical alternative-access methods [27]. Major complications, although rare, include retroperitoneal hematoma, aortic dissection, persistent arteriovenous fistula (AVF), and device embolization [28]. Routine post-closure aortography is performed to ensure complete seal and exclude major extravasation. Over time, the retroperitoneal tract endothelizes, and most residual minor AVFs close spontaneously during mid-term follow-up without requiring further intervention [29].

### Future Horizons and Conclusions
Transcaval access has expanded beyond TAVR to support other large-bore interventions, including thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR), endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), and the insertion of percutaneous mechanical circulatory support devices like the Impella [10, 30]. Continued refinements in dedicated transcaval closure devices and standardized crossing techniques promise to further lower the learning curve and minimize vascular complications. In conclusion, transcaval access represents a major paradigm shift in structural heart interventions, providing a safe, entirely percutaneous conduit for patients ineligible for conventional transfemoral access.
